💡 The Intuitive Big Picture

How Do Banks Use AI to Decide Loans Without Breaking the Law?

Every day, banks receive thousands of loan applications. If they lend to someone who defaults (doesn't pay back), the bank loses money. But if they use a "black-box" AI that just says "Denied" without reasons, they violate federal consumer financial protection laws (ECOA & FCRA).

✓ Predictive Accuracy with Tuned Tree Ensembles
✓ Honest Probabilities with Platt Scaling Calibration
✓ Legally Auditable Reasons with SHAP Game Theory
1

The Bank's Dilemma

Out of 1,000 borrowers in our dataset, 700 repay on time and 300 default. Blindly rejecting people destroys customer loyalty, while approving bad loans leads to balance sheet write-offs. We need an intelligent, automated risk engine.

2

The Legal Mandate (FCRA & ECOA)

Under ECOA (Regulation B) and FCRA § 615(a), banks are legally prohibited from discriminating and must issue an Adverse Action Notice giving the top 4 specific financial factors that caused a loan denial.

3

Our 3-Tier Underwriting Protocol

Instead of binary yes/no, our system implements a smart 3-tier triage:
• P < 30%: Auto-Approve (Fast track)
• 30% ≤ P ≤ 65%: Human Underwriter Review
• P > 65%: Auto-Decline + SHAP Adverse Reasons

📚 From First Principles to Advanced Math

Machine Learning Theory Explained with Everyday Analogies

If you missed classes, don't worry. Machine learning is just teaching a computer to recognize patterns from past experience. Here are the core concepts that power this project.

⚖️

1. The Class Imbalance Trap

Why simple accuracy will ruin your bank

Our dataset has 700 good borrowers (70%) and 300 bad borrowers (30%).

If a lazy AI just says "Everyone is good" for all 1,000 people, it gets 70% accuracy! The teacher would think it's decent, but the bank would lose millions on all 300 defaulters.

How we solve it in this project:
• Class-Weighted Loss: We multiply the loss penalty on minority default errors by w1 = N_0 / N_1 ≈ 2.33. The AI gets punished 2.33x harder if it misses a default.
• SMOTE: Creates synthetic, realistic artificial default examples along lines connecting neighboring default records.
🌲

2. Logistic Regression vs Tree Ensembles

Linear models vs Gradient Boosted Trees

Logistic Regression: Draws a smooth single hyperplane separating good and bad applicants. Great baseline, but cannot easily capture complex non-linear combinations (e.g. young age + high debt).

Random Forest: A "parliament" of 200 independent trees voting. Reduces variance (overfitting).

XGBoost / LightGBM: A team where each new tree specifically trains on the residual errors of the previous trees. This won the highest PR-AUC (0.6650).

📈

3. Platt Scaling (Probability Calibration)

Turning raw scores into honest probabilities

XGBoost outputs a margin f(x). If the model is uncalibrated, a raw score of 0.85 might only mean a 60% real-world default rate!

P(Y=1 | f(x)) = 1 / (1 + exp(A • f(x) + B))

Platt scaling fits a post-hoc logistic transformation over cross-validation holdouts. This reduced our Brier Score from 0.1740 → 0.1570 (a 9.7% improvement in risk honesty).

🔍

4. SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations)

Nobel Prize economics applied to AI transparency

Imagine a soccer team wins 3-1. How much credit goes to the striker vs goalkeeper? Lloyd Shapley invented Shapley Values (1953) to fairly share credit in cooperative games.

In our model, the "players" are features (Duration, Checking Status, Age). SHAP proves mathematically that:

f(x) = E[f(x)] + ∑ φi(x)

The total prediction equals the base risk plus each feature's marginal contribution!

💻 Production Python Architecture

How the Source Code is Structured & How It Runs

The project is engineered into modular, clean Python files inside src/ and accompanied by the full interactive lab notebook notebooks/Credit_Default_Risk_Prediction_SHAP.ipynb.

Data Leakage Prevention & ColumnTransformer

Notice how fit_transform is only called on the training data. The test data is only transformed using the learned parameters. 

# src/preprocessing.py
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE

class CreditDataPreprocessor:
    def __init__(self):
        # Numerical Pipeline: Median imputation + Z-Score standardization
        self.num_pipeline = Pipeline([
            ('imputer', SimpleImputer(strategy='median')),
            ('scaler', StandardScaler())
        ])
        
        # Categorical Pipeline: Most-frequent imputation + One-Hot Encoding
        self.cat_pipeline = Pipeline([
            ('imputer', SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent')),
            ('encoder', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', sparse_output=False))
        ])
        
        self.column_transformer = ColumnTransformer(
            transformers=[
                ('num', self.num_pipeline, NUMERICAL_FEATURES),
                ('cat', self.cat_pipeline, CATEGORICAL_FEATURES)
            ]
        )

    def fit_transform(self, X_train):
        # Strictly fit statistics only on the training set!
        return self.column_transformer.fit_transform(X_train)

    def transform(self, X_test):
        # Apply fitted statistics to test set without peeking
        return self.column_transformer.transform(X_test)

Model Tuning with Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation

We use scale_pos_weight=2.33 for XGBoost and class_weight='balanced' for Random Forest to tackle class imbalance. 

# src/models.py
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold

def get_xgb_pipeline():
    # Scale pos weight = 700 / 300 = 2.333 (penalty for missing defaults)
    xgb = XGBClassifier(
        scale_pos_weight=2.333,
        eval_metric='logloss',
        random_state=42
    )
    param_grid = {
        'max_depth': [3, 4, 6],
        'learning_rate': [0.01, 0.05, 0.1],
        'n_estimators': [100, 200],
        'subsample': [0.8, 1.0]
    }
    cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
    return GridSearchCV(xgb, param_grid, cv=cv, scoring='roc_auc', n_jobs=-1)

Probability Calibration via Platt Scaling

Using Scikit-Learn's CalibratedClassifierCV(method='sigmoid', cv=5) to map uncalibrated tree margins to true probabilities. 

# src/calibration.py
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss

def calibrate_model(base_estimator, X_train, y_train, method='sigmoid', cv=5):
    # Fits Platt sigmoid calibration curves across internal CV folds
    calibrated = CalibratedClassifierCV(
        estimator=base_estimator,
        method=method,
        cv=cv
    )
    calibrated.fit(X_train, y_train)
    return calibrated

def compute_calibration_metrics(y_true, p_uncal, p_cal):
    brier_uncal = brier_score_loss(y_true, p_uncal)
    brier_cal = brier_score_loss(y_true, p_cal)
    improvement = ((brier_uncal - brier_cal) / brier_uncal) * 100
    return {
        'brier_uncal': brier_uncal,
        'brier_cal': brier_cal,
        'improvement_pct': improvement
    }

TreeExplainer & Regulatory Adverse Action Generation

Extracts top SHAP factors and maps encoded feature names to official human-readable disclosure statements. 

# src/explainability.py
import shap

class CreditRiskExplainer:
    def __init__(self, model, feature_names):
        self.explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)
        self.feature_names = feature_names

    def explain_instance(self, sample_row):
        # Calculate exact Shapley values for this specific applicant
        shap_values = self.explainer(sample_row)
        
        # Sort factors pushing risk upwards (+ positive SHAP)
        risk_drivers = []
        for feat_name, val, impact in zip(self.feature_names, sample_row, shap_values.values[0]):
            if impact > 0:
                risk_drivers.append((feat_name, impact, val))
        
        risk_drivers.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
        top_reasons = risk_drivers[:4] # Legally required Top 4 Adverse Reasons
        return top_reasons

End-to-End Orchestrator (run_pipeline)

Runs all 7 stages seamlessly: ingestion → preprocessing → tuning → calibration → evaluation → SHAP → figure output. 

# src/pipeline.py
def run_pipeline():
    # 1. Load Data
    df_raw = load_raw_data(RAW_DATA_PATH)
    X_train_raw, X_test_raw, y_train, y_test, metadata = prepare_data(df_raw)
    
    # 2. Preprocess
    preprocessor = CreditDataPreprocessor()
    X_train = preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train_raw)
    X_test = preprocessor.transform(X_test_raw)
    
    # 3. Model Training & Cross-Validation
    models_dict = tune_and_train_models(X_train, y_train)
    
    # 4. Platt Calibration
    calibrated_models = {name: calibrate_model(m, X_train, y_train) for name, m in models_dict.items()}
    
    # 5. Evaluate & Generate Figures
    eval_df = evaluate_models(calibrated_models, X_test, y_test)
    
    # 6. SHAP Analysis
    explainer = CreditRiskExplainer(calibrated_models['XGBoost'], preprocessor.feature_names_)
    explainer.generate_all_reports()
    print("Pipeline Complete! All figures generated in reports/figures/")
🎯 University Exam & Viva Defense

The Top 10 Questions Your Teacher Will Ask (With Answers)

Click any card to reveal the exact, polished technical response you should give to your examiner.

Q1. Why did you use ROC-AUC and PR-AUC instead of simple Accuracy?

+

Perfect Answer: "In credit risk, classes are heavily imbalanced (70% good, 30% bad). If a model simply predicts 'Good' for every applicant, it gets 70% accuracy while failing to detect 100% of defaults! ROC-AUC measures discriminatory ability across all thresholds, and PR-AUC explicitly measures precision and recall on the rare default class. Our champion XGBoost achieved the highest PR-AUC of 0.665."

Q2. What is Data Leakage and how did you prevent it in your code?

+

Perfect Answer: "Data leakage happens when information from outside the training dataset is inadvertently used to create the model—for example, calculating the mean, median, or scaling statistics across all 1,000 applicants before splitting. We strictly performed a Stratified 80/20 train/test split first, and fitted our imputers, scalers, and encoders exclusively on X_train. The test set was transformed using only training statistics."

Q3. Why do tree models need Platt Scaling? Don't they already output probabilities?

+

Perfect Answer: "Gradient boosted trees output leaf scores that are excellent for ranking relative risk, but uncalibrated in a statistical sense; they tend to push probabilities toward extreme values or cluster in narrow ranges. Platt scaling fits a cross-validated logistic sigmoid mapping raw margins to empirical default rates. This reduced our Brier score from 0.1740 to 0.1570 (a 9.7% improvement), ensuring that a 30% score actually means 3 out of 10 people default."

Q4. What is the difference between SMOTE and Class-Weighted Loss? Which was better?

+

Perfect Answer: "SMOTE synthesizes new artificial minority points using k-nearest neighbors in feature space before training. Class-weighted loss modifies the algorithm's loss function directly by penalizing minority misclassifications with a higher multiplier (w1 = 2.33). In our experiments, Class-Weighted XGBoost achieved a higher PR-AUC (0.665 vs 0.651) with less distortion of feature distributions than SMOTE."

Q5. Why is SHAP superior to standard Gini feature importance?

+

Perfect Answer: "Standard Gini feature importance only provides a macro-level metric of how frequently a feature was split on, and it is heavily biased toward continuous variables with high cardinality. Most importantly, Gini cannot explain individual predictions. SHAP is grounded in cooperative game theory (satisfying Efficiency, Symmetry, and Additivity axioms) and provides local waterfall attributions for specific applicants, enabling automated legal Adverse Action disclosures."

Q6. Explain the 3-Tier Underwriting Decision Policy.

+

Perfect Answer: "Rather than an arbitrary 0.50 binary threshold, we establish three operational tiers: 1. P < 0.30: Tier 1 Auto-Approve (Low risk, instant fulfillment). 2. 0.30 ≤ P ≤ 0.65: Tier 2 Human Review (High model uncertainty zone, routed to a human underwriter). 3. P > 0.65: Tier 3 Auto-Decline (High risk, automated FCRA Adverse Action Statement generated with top 4 SHAP drivers)."
